problem: Existing audio-event datasets (ESC, AudioSet, FSD50K) lack spatial/3D context, and audio-visual datasets are limited to images/videos, so there is no large-scale resource linking audio events to objects in 3D scenes.
motivation: Audio carries information that disambiguates sound sources and is valuable for HCI, monitoring and robotics, but studying audio-conditioned 3D tasks needs audio aligned to object locations in scenes. Purely manual annotation does not scale, while LLM commonsense can propose object-event associations that humans then verify.
key_idea: Use GPT-4 to generate object-event pairs and map them to unified event labels across four audio datasets, verify them with humans, and attach the audio to object locations in ScanNet and RoboTHOR scenes to create Audio-ScanNet and Audio-RoboTHOR.
insight: LLM commonsense plus dual GPT-4/human scoring (both scores >3) gives a scalable way to build object-audio associations. Benchmarks show that text-based 3D grounding and ZSON methods with a swapped-in audio encoder (wav2clip) perform poorly (e.g., 3DVG-Transformer mAP@0.25 of 0.084), so audio-conditioned spatial tasks remain hard. A pipeline that recognizes the event, detects objects, and lets an LLM reason about the sound source does best on average, although it loses to MVT on visually specific objects such as bed or refrigerator. No ablations are reported.
method: Category selection: pick 36 object categories common to ScanNet and RoboTHOR (e.g., alarmclock, apple, bed).
LLM-OEG: prompt GPT-4 to infer plausible sound events per object category, followed by manual review of each event's plausibility.

Event normalization and mapping: GPT-4 merges semantically similar labels across ESC-50, FSD50K, EPIC-SOUNDS and ReaLISED into unified names, then produces a 1-5 relevance score matrix M_GPT4 between generated and dataset events; a human matrix M_Human is built, and pairs scoring >3 in both are kept.
Audio-to-scene mapping: index object categories to audio clips and attach the clips to the spatial coordinates of the objects in the scenes, giving 12,876 clips, 65 events and 36 categories.
Grounding baselines: 3DVG-Transformer, 3D-SPS and Multi-View Transformer with the text encoder replaced by a wav2clip audio encoder.
Proposed grounding method: wav2clip audio-to-event recognition, VoteNet object detection, and LLaMA to infer which detected object most likely produced the sound.
Audio navigation baselines: wav2clip plus an MLP (512->384->k) classifies audio into an object category, which is fed to zero-shot object navigation models (CoW CLIP variants, MDETR, OWL, ESC).

setting.backbone: Grounding: wav2clip + VoteNet + LLaMA; Navigation: wav2clip audio classifier (MLP) + zero-shot ObjNav baselines (CLIP variants, MDETR, OWL-ViT, ESC with GLIP + LLM)
setting.training_data: Audio-ScanNet / Audio-RoboTHOR (12,876 clips from ESC, FSD50K, EPIC-SOUNDS, ReaLISED mapped to 36 object categories); navigation models are zero-shot with a trained audio classifier
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB(-D) in RoboTHOR; ScanNet point clouds for grounding; audio clip as goal
setting.action_space: Not specified (standard ZSON discrete actions with STOP)
setting.privileged: none stated (audio goal is classified into an object category)

numbers.method: ESC (best baseline; the paper proposes no navigation method of its own)
numbers.backbone: GLIP + LLM with wav2clip audio classifier
numbers.extra: audio goal converted to a category label by wav2clip+MLP; success radius 1.0 m; split not stated
numbers.evidence: Table: quantitative results for audio-based object navigation on RoboTHOR, ESC row 14.1 / 27.1
Table: Performance comparison of audio-based object grounding on ScanNet, mAP row

numbers_note: Navigation baselines are compared on RoboTHOR with SR/SPL only; the dataset split is not specified. Grounding table values are printed as fractions (0.429), kept as printed.
results: On audio-based 3D grounding, the proposed pipeline reaches mAP@0.25 of 0.429 and mAP@0.5 of 0.391, beating MVT (0.360/0.274), 3D-SPS and 3DVG-Transformer. On audio-goal navigation, ESC is best (SR 27.1, SPL 14.1) ahead of CLIP-OWL (21.9/13.4), while low absolute scores show the tasks remain hard.
limitations: Benchmarks are simple adaptations (text encoder swapped for wav2clip), audio is mapped only to object categories rather than realistically spatialized, and the paper reports no ablations or analysis of the dataset construction.
Navigation uses a classifier to convert audio to a category label, so it becomes text ObjNav. No new navigation method is proposed, and the split and number of episodes are not given.
Human verification details such as inter-annotator agreement are claimed in the abstract but not reported in the text.
